claim: Pancreatic KATP channel trafficking defects underlie congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI) cases unresponsive to the KATP channel opener diazoxide.
source: Pancreatic KATP channel trafficking defects underlie congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI) cases unresponsive to the KATP channel opener diazoxide, the mainstay medical therapy for CHI.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about CHI and KATP channel trafficking defects.

claim: Diazoxide is the mainstay medical therapy for CHI.
source: Pancreatic KATP channel trafficking defects underlie congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI) cases unresponsive to the KATP channel opener diazoxide, the mainstay medical therapy for CHI.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established medical knowledge.

claim: Current clinically used KATP channel inhibitors act as pharmacochaperones and restore surface expression of trafficking mutants.
source: Current clinically used KATP channel inhibitors have been shown to act as pharmacochaperones and restore surface expression of trafficking mutants; however, their therapeutic utility for KATP trafficking-impaired CHI is hindered by high affinity binding, which limits functional recovery of rescued channels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge from prior research.

claim: High affinity binding of current KATP channel inhibitors limits functional recovery of rescued channels.
source: Current clinically used KATP channel inhibitors have been shown to act as pharmacochaperones and restore surface expression of trafficking mutants; however, their therapeutic utility for KATP trafficking-impaired CHI is hindered by high affinity binding, which limits functional recovery of rescued channels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a limitation of current pharmacochaperones.

claim: Recent structural studies of KATP channels employing cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) have revealed a promiscuous pocket where several known KATP pharmacochaperones bind.
source: Recent structural studies of KATP channels employing cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) have revealed a promiscuous pocket where several known KATP pharmacochaperones bind.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background from recent structural studies.

claim: Aekatperone was identified using an AI-based virtual screening technology AtomNet followed by functional validation.
source: Using an AI-based virtual screening technology AtomNet followed by functional validation, we identified a novel compound, termed Aekatperone, which exhibits chaperoning effects on KATP channel trafficking mutations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Aekatperone exhibits chaperoning effects on KATP channel trafficking mutations.
source: Using an AI-based virtual screening technology AtomNet followed by functional validation, we identified a novel compound, termed Aekatperone, which exhibits chaperoning effects on KATP channel trafficking mutations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Aekatperone reversibly inhibits KATP channel activity with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) ~9 μM.
source: Aekatperone reversibly inhibits KATP channel activity with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) ~9 μM.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutant channels rescued to the cell surface by Aekatperone showed functional recovery upon washout of the compound.
source: Mutant channels rescued to the cell surface by Aekatperone showed functional recovery upon washout of the compound.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: CryoEM structure of KATP bound to Aekatperone revealed distinct binding features compared to known high affinity inhibitor pharmacochaperones.
source: CryoEM structure of KATP bound to Aekatperone revealed distinct binding features compared to known high affinity inhibitor pharmacochaperones.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding supported by structural data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Pancreatic β-cells secrete insulin in response to an increase in blood glucose levels to maintain glucose homeostasis.
source: Pancreatic β-cells secrete insulin in response to an increase in blood glucose levels to maintain glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established physiological knowledge.

claim: The ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel is assembled from four pore-forming Kir6.2 subunits and four regulatory SUR1 subunits.
source: Central to this process is the ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel assembled from four pore-forming Kir6.2 subunits (encoded by KCNJ11) and four regulatory SUR1 subunits (encoded by ABCC8) (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999; Ashcroft, 2023; Driggers and Shyng, 2023; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Kir6.2 is encoded by KCNJ11.
source: Central to this process is the ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel assembled from four pore-forming Kir6.2 subunits (encoded by KCNJ11) and four regulatory SUR1 subunits (encoded by ABCC8) (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999; Ashcroft, 2023; Driggers and Shyng, 2023; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SUR1 is encoded by ABCC8.
source: Central to this process is the ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel assembled from four pore-forming Kir6.2 subunits (encoded by KCNJ11) and four regulatory SUR1 subunits (encoded by ABCC8) (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999; Ashcroft, 2023; Driggers and Shyng, 2023; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: KATP channels are gated by intracellular ATP and ADP.
source: KATP channels are gated by intracellular ATP and ADP, the concentrations of which change following glucose metabolism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about KATP channel function.

claim: When serum blood glucose levels rise, the intracellular ATP/ADP ratio increases, which promotes KATP channel closure.
source: When serum blood glucose levels rise, the intracellular ATP/ADP ratio increases, which promotes KATP channel closure, membrane depolarization, Ca2+ influx through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and insulin secretion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established physiological mechanism.

claim: Gain-of-function KATP mutations cause neonatal diabetes.
source: Underscoring the importance of β-cell KATP channels in glucose regulation, gain-of-function KATP mutations cause neonatal diabetes, while loss-of-function KATP mutations cause congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI) (Ashcroft, 2023; De Franco et al., 2020; ElSheikh and Shyng, 2023; Nichols et al., 2022; Pipatpolkai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Loss-of-function KATP mutations cause congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI).
source: Underscoring the importance of β-cell KATP channels in glucose regulation, gain-of-function KATP mutations cause neonatal diabetes, while loss-of-function KATP mutations cause congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI) (Ashcroft, 2023; De Franco et al., 2020; ElSheikh and Shyng, 2023; Nichols et al., 2022; Pipatpolkai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: CHI caused by mutations in ABCC8 or KCNJ11 that prevent proper folding and assembly of the channel proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and subsequent trafficking of KATP channels to the β-cell plasma membrane.
source: A case in point is CHI caused by mutations in ABCC8 or KCNJ11 that prevent proper folding and assembly of the channel proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and subsequent trafficking of KATP channels to the β-cell plasma membrane (Cartier et al., 2001; Crane and Aguilar-Bryan, 2004; ElSheikh and Shyng, 2023; Fukuda et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Individuals harboring trafficking mutations present severe CHI disease unresponsive to diazoxide and often require pancreatectomy to prevent life-threatening hypoglycemia.
source: Individuals harboring such mutations present severe CHI disease unresponsive to diazoxide and often require pancreatectomy to prevent life-threatening hypoglycemia.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as clinical knowledge about CHI patients with trafficking mutations.

claim: Pharmacological chaperones (pharmacochaperones) are small molecules that bind to target proteins and facilitate their folding, assembly, and trafficking.
source: Pharmacological chaperones (pharmacochaperones) are small molecules that bind to target proteins and facilitate their folding, assembly, and trafficking (Bernier et al., 2004; Convertino et al., 2016; Leidenheimer and Ryder, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: KATP channel inhibitors act as pharmacochaperones to overcome KATP trafficking defects.
source: Previous work has shown that KATP channel inhibitors act as pharmacochaperones to overcome KATP trafficking defects (Martin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Glibenclamide (GBC) is a high affinity sulfonylurea that has long been used clinically for type 2 diabetes.
source: Among these inhibitor pharmacochaperones, glibenclamide (GBC), a high affinity sulfonylurea, and repaglinide (RPG), a high affinity glinide, have long been used clinically for type 2 diabetes (Sahin et al., 2024);
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Repaglinide (RPG) is a high affinity glinide that has long been used clinically for type 2 diabetes.
source: Among these inhibitor pharmacochaperones, glibenclamide (GBC), a high affinity sulfonylurea, and repaglinide (RPG), a high affinity glinide, have long been used clinically for type 2 diabetes (Sahin et al., 2024);
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Carbamazepine (CBZ), an anticonvulsant known to inhibit voltage-gated Na+ channel, has been found to potently inhibit KATP channels.
source: in addition, carbamazepine (CBZ), an anticonvulsant known to inhibit voltage-gated Na+ channel, has been found to potently inhibit KATP channels (Chen et al., 2013; Devaraneni et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Kir6.2 is a transmembrane (TM) protein with two TM helices and cytoplasmic N- and C-termini.
source: Kir6.2 is a transmembrane (TM) protein with two TM helices and cytoplasmic N- and C-termini.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as structural knowledge about Kir6.2.

claim: SUR1 is a member of the ABC protein family.
source: SUR1, a member of the ABC protein family, consists of a canonical ABC core structure of two 6-TM helix TM domains (TMD), TMD1 and TMD2, and two cytoplasmic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs), NBD1 and NBD2;
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as structural knowledge about SUR1.

claim: SUR1 consists of a canonical ABC core structure of two 6-TM helix TM domains (TMD), TMD1 and TMD2, and two cytoplasmic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs), NBD1 and NBD2.
source: SUR1, a member of the ABC protein family, consists of a canonical ABC core structure of two 6-TM helix TM domains (TMD), TMD1 and TMD2, and two cytoplasmic nucleotide binding domains (NBDs), NBD1 and NBD2;
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as structural knowledge about SUR1.

claim: SUR1 contains an N-terminal TM domain TMD0 which is connected to the ABC core via a cytoplasmic linker, L0.
source: in addition, it contains an N-terminal TM domain TMD0 which is connected to the ABC core via a cytoplasmic linker, L0 (Driggers and Shyng, 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: KATP inhibitors bind at a common pocket in the TMD of the SUR1-ABC core that serves to anchor and immobilize the Kir6.2 N-terminus.
source: Recent high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) structures of KATP channels along with functional studies revealed that KATP inhibitors bind at a common pocket in the TMD of the SUR1-ABC core that serves to anchor and immobilize the Kir6.2 N-terminus, which interaction stabilizes nascent channel assembly and hence trafficking to the cell surface (Martin et al., 2017a; Martin et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The SUR1-Kir6.2 interaction stabilizes nascent channel assembly and hence trafficking to the cell surface.
source: Recent high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) structures of KATP channels along with functional studies revealed that KATP inhibitors bind at a common pocket in the TMD of the SUR1-ABC core that serves to anchor and immobilize the Kir6.2 N-terminus, which interaction stabilizes nascent channel assembly and hence trafficking to the cell surface (Martin et al., 2017a; Martin et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The same SUR1-Kir6.2 interaction results in channel closure.
source: Paradoxically, the same SUR1-Kir6.2 interaction also results in channel closure, explaining the dual pharmacochaperone and inhibitory effects of the aforementioned compounds.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from structural and functional studies.

claim: Virtual screening of ~2.5 million small organic molecules in the Enamine in-stock library was performed against the binding site of repaglinide (RPG) in the RPG-bound KATP channel cryoEM structure (PDB ID 6PZ9).
source: Using an Artificial Intelligence (AI) virtual screening system AtomNet developed by Atomwise (Atomwise AIMS Program, 2024; Gniewek et al., 2021; Wallach et al., 2015), we performed virtual screening of ~2.5 million small organic molecules in the Enamine in-stock library against the binding site of a high affinity KATP inhibitor pharmacochaperone, RPG, resolved in our published RPG-bound KATP channel (hamster SUR1 plus rat Kir6.2) cryoEM structure (PDB ID 6PZ9; ~3.65 Å) (Atomwise AIMS Program, 2024; Martin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the virtual screening methodology.

claim: The RPG binding site being screened involves the following residues: R306, Y377, A380, I381, W430, F433, L434, N437, M441, T588, L592, L593, S595, V596, T1242, N1245, R1246, E1249, W1297, R1300 of the SUR1 subunit and residues M1, L2, S3, K5, G6, I7 of Kir6.2.
source: The RPG binding site being screened involves the following residues: R306, Y377, A380, I381, W430, F433, L434, N437, M441, T588, L592, L593, S595, V596, T1242, N1245, R1246, E1249, W1297, R1300 of the SUR1 subunit (chain C in PDB ID 6PZ9) and residues M1, L2, S3, K5, G6, I7 of Kir6.2 (chain D in PDB ID 6PZ9) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The top 96 predicted binders were subjected to biochemical and functional testing.
source: Following diversity clustering to minimize selection of structurally similar scaffolds and filtering for oral availability as well as excluding toxicophores (see Methods for details), the top 96 predicted binders (Supplementary file 1) were subjected to subsequent biochemical and functional testing as described below.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the experimental workflow.

claim: Three compounds (C24, C27, and C45) showed consistent pharmacochaperone effects in two independent screening experiments.
source: Treatment with some of the test compounds yielded weak or moderate upper SUR1F27S band, suggesting pharmacochaperone effects. We selected three compounds that showed consistent results in two independent screening experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) for further testing in a different assay.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: C24, C27, and C45 correspond to ZINC IDs Z1607618869, Z2068224500, and Z1620764636, respectively.
source: The three compounds selected, C24, C27, and C45, correspond to ZINC database (https://zinc.docking.org/) ID: Z1607618869, Z2068224500, and Z1620764636, respectively, and represent diverse chemical scaffolds, as shown in Figure 1B.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All three compounds (C24, C27, and C45) inhibited KATP channel currents.
source: Inside-out patch-clamp recordings of cells expressing KATP channels (hamster WT SUR1+rat WT Kir6.2) showed that indeed, all three compounds inhibited KATP channel currents (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Compound Z1620764636 (C45) showed a clear dose-dependent inhibition, with an estimated steady-state IC50 between 1 and 10 μM, and clear current recovery upon compound washout.
source: Of the three compounds Z1620764636 (C45) showed a clear dose-dependent inhibition, with an estimated steady-state IC50 between 1 and 10 μM, and clear current recovery upon compound washout (Figure 1—figure supplement 2Ci).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2Ci.

claim: Overnight treatment with 100 μM Aekatperone led to a clear increase of the mature upper band for SUR1A30T, SUR1A116P, and SUR1V187D trafficking mutants.
source: Overnight treatment with 100 μM Aekatperone led to a clear increase of the mature upper band (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The pharmacochaperone effect of Aekatperone on SUR1A30T was already evident at 10 μM and became more pronounced as the concentration increased, with the effect plateauing between 100 and 200 μM.
source: A detailed dose-response for SUR1A30T showed that the pharmacochaperone effect of Aekatperone was already evident at 10 μM and became more pronounced as the concentration increased, with the effect plateauing between 100 and 200 μM (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At 200 μM Aekatperone, the intensity of the upper band relative to the total intensity of both lower and upper bands for SUR1A30T was 64.21 ± 3.35% of that observed for WT SUR1.
source: At 200 μM, the intensity of the upper band relative to the total intensity of both lower and upper bands for SUR1A30T was 64.21 ± 3.35% of that observed for WT SUR1 (n=3, p=0.0133 by Student's t-test) based on densitometry by ImageJ (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Upon Aekatperone treatment, there was a clear increase in the percentage of cells showing surface staining of SUR1F27S or SUR1A30T mutant channels.
source: Upon Aekatperone treatment, there was a clear increase in the percentage of cells showing surface staining of SUR1F27S or SUR1A30T mutant channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, top panels), providing direct evidence that Aekatperone rescues surface expression of CHI-causing SUR1 trafficking mutations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inclusion of 10 μM Aekatperone occluded the stimulatory effect of MgADP on KATP channels.
source: Inclusion of 10 μM Aekatperone occluded the stimulatory effect of MgADP, but MgADP stimulation recovered upon subsequent removal of Aekatperone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MgADP stimulation recovered upon subsequent removal of Aekatperone.
source: Inclusion of 10 μM Aekatperone occluded the stimulatory effect of MgADP, but MgADP stimulation recovered upon subsequent removal of Aekatperone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The pharmacochaperone effects of Aekatperone on trafficking mutants and reversible inhibitory effect of Aekatperone on channel response to MgADP were also observed in channels formed by human SUR1 and human Kir6.2.
source: Importantly, the pharmacochaperone effects of Aekatperone on trafficking mutants and reversible inhibitory effect of Aekatperone on channel response to MgADP were also observed in channels formed by human SUR1 and human Kir6.2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which are highly homologous to hamster SUR1 and rat Kir6.2 at the protein level (95% and 96%, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Human SUR1 and human Kir6.2 are highly homologous to hamster SUR1 and rat Kir6.2 at the protein level (95% and 96%, respectively).
source: Importantly, the pharmacochaperone effects of Aekatperone on trafficking mutants and reversible inhibitory effect of Aekatperone on channel response to MgADP were also observed in channels formed by human SUR1 and human Kir6.2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which are highly homologous to hamster SUR1 and rat Kir6.2 at the protein level (95% and 96%, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison of protein sequences.

claim: Aekatperone dose-dependently reduced Rb+ efflux in WT KATP channels, with an IC50 of 9.23 µM±0.36 µM.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, Aekatperone dose-dependently reduced Rb+ efflux, with an IC50 of 9.23 µM±0.36 µM (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Rb+ efflux assay data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: For both SUR1F27S and SUR1A30T mutants, a significant increase in Rb+ efflux was observed in cells treated with Aekatperone in a dose-dependent manner compared with cells treated with 0.1% DMSO.
source: Under these conditions, we observed for both mutants a significant increase in Rb+ efflux in cells treated with Aekatperone in a dose-dependent manner compared with cells treated with 0.1% DMSO (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Rb+ efflux assay data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Cells treated overnight with the high affinity inhibitor pharmacochaperone GBC followed by 30 min incubation in medium lacking GBC showed Rb+ efflux below that seen in cells treated overnight with the DMSO vehicle control.
source: This is in stark contrast to cells treated overnight with the high affinity inhibitor pharmacochaperone GBC followed by 30 min incubation in medium lacking GBC, where Rb+ efflux was below that seen in cells treated overnight with the DMSO vehicle control (note in DMSO-treated controls, there were still low levels of surface expression of the mutant channels to give rise to the low levels of efflux).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison between Aekatperone and GBC effects.

claim: Mutant-expressing cells treated overnight with Aekatperone followed by subsequent drug removal showed much greater diazoxide response, achieving up to 80% of the WT response.
source: Significantly, mutant-expressing cells treated overnight with Aekatperone followed by subsequent drug removal showed much greater diazoxide response, achieving up to 80% of the WT response.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Rb+ efflux assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Including 10 μM Aekatperone had no significant effects on MgADP stimulation of SUR2A/Kir6.2 nor SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels.
source: Inside-out patch-clamp recordings showed that including 10 μM Aekatperone had no significant effects on MgADP stimulation of SUR2A/Kir6.2 nor SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 4A), indicating SUR2A/Kir6.2 and SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels are relatively insensitive to Aekatperone compared to SUR1/Kir6.2 channels.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Aekatperone IC50 is 41.22 µM±2.22 µM for SUR2A/Kir6.2 channels and 41.85 µM±2.08 µM for SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels.
source: The results yielded dose-response curves showing an Aekatperone IC50 of 41.22 µM±2.22 µM for SUR2A/Kir6.2 channels and 41.85 µM±2.08 µM for SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 4B), which are more than fourfold higher than the IC50 of 9.2 µM for SUR1/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Rb+ efflux assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Aekatperone IC50 for SUR2A/Kir6.2 and SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels are more than fourfold higher than the IC50 of 9.2 µM for SUR1/Kir6.2 channels.
source: The results yielded dose-response curves showing an Aekatperone IC50 of 41.22 µM±2.22 µM for SUR2A/Kir6.2 channels and 41.85 µM±2.08 µM for SUR2B/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 4B), which are more than fourfold higher than the IC50 of 9.2 µM for SUR1/Kir6.2 channels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 4B.

claim: 3D reconstruction of cryoEM particles of channels incubated with Aekatperone yielded a map with an overall resolution of 4.1 Å.
source: 3D reconstruction of cryoEM particles of channels incubated with Aekatperone yielded a map with an overall resolution of 4.1 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the cryoEM structure determination.

claim: A model built from the cryoEM map shows a closed Kir6.2 channel pore with a pore radius of ~0.75 Å at the helical bundle crossing residue F168 and an inward-facing SUR1 with NBDs separated.
source: A model built from the map shows a closed Kir6.2 channel pore with a pore radius of ~0.75 Å at the helical bundle crossing residue F168 and an inward-facing SUR1 with NBDs separated, resembling other inhibitor-bound KATP channel structures reported to date (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the cryoEM structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A clear nonprotein density consistent with the size of Aekatperone (MW: 399.52 g/mol) was observed in a TM pocket above NBD1 in the ABC core of SUR1.
source: A clear nonprotein density consistent with the size of Aekatperone (MW: 399.52 g/mol) was observed in a TM pocket above NBD1 in the ABC core of SUR1 (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the cryoEM density shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Clear cryoEM density corresponding to the Kir6.2 distal N-terminal peptide domain (KNtp) was observed in between the two TM bundles of the SUR1-ABC core, with the very N-terminus of Kir6.2 contacting the bound Aekatperone.
source: Moreover, as in the structures of KATP bound to GBC, RPG, or CBZ (Martin et al., 2019; Sung et al., 2022), we observed clear cryoEM density corresponding to the Kir6.2 distal N-terminal peptide domain (KNtp) in between the two TM bundles of the SUR1-ABC core, with the very N-terminus of Kir6.2 contacting the bound Aekatperone (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the cryoEM structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Stabilization of the KNtp-SUR1 interface promotes channel assembly, at the same time, it prevents Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain from rotating to an open conformation.
source: Stabilization of the KNtp-SUR1 interface promotes channel assembly, at the same time, it prevents Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain from rotating to an open conformation (Driggers et al., 2024; Martin et al., 2019; Sung et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2018), which explains the dual chaperone and inhibitor activity of Aekatperone.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The cyclohexyl moiety of Aekatperone is aligned with S1238 on the cytoplasmic end of the binding pocket.
source: In this structural model, the cyclohexyl moiety of Aekatperone is aligned with S1238 on the cytoplasmic end of the binding pocket, and the imidazole group is oriented toward the extracellular end of the binding pocket, interacting with the distal part of KNtp.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the Aekatperone binding conformation.

claim: The imidazole group of Aekatperone is oriented toward the extracellular end of the binding pocket, interacting with the distal part of KNtp.
source: In this structural model, the cyclohexyl moiety of Aekatperone is aligned with S1238 on the cytoplasmic end of the binding pocket, and the imidazole group is oriented toward the extracellular end of the binding pocket, interacting with the distal part of KNtp.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the Aekatperone binding conformation.

claim: The pyrazole moiety of Aekatperone has its two nitrogen atoms coordinated by T1242 and N1245.
source: The pyrazole moiety has its two nitrogen atoms coordinated by T1242 and N1245, while the sulfonyl moiety is oriented toward R1246 and R1300, each interacts with one of the two oxygens of the sulfonyl group.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the Aekatperone binding interactions.

claim: The sulfonyl moiety of Aekatperone is oriented toward R1246 and R1300, each interacts with one of the two oxygens of the sulfonyl group.
source: The pyrazole moiety has its two nitrogen atoms coordinated by T1242 and N1245, while the sulfonyl moiety is oriented toward R1246 and R1300, each interacts with one of the two oxygens of the sulfonyl group.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the Aekatperone binding interactions.

claim: The benzene ring of Aekatperone forms a π–π stacking interaction with Y377 of SUR1.
source: Moreover, the benzene ring of Aekatperone forms a π–π stacking interaction with Y377 of SUR1, and a series of hydrophobic interactions contributed by TM helices from both TMD1 (TM6, 7) and TMD2 (TM16, 17) help stabilize the benzene and cyclohexyl groups.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the Aekatperone binding interactions.

claim: Unlike GBC and RPG, Aekatperone does not reach far into the extracellular end of the pocket to interact with R306.
source: Interestingly, unlike GBC and RPG, the binding of both involves R306 of SUR1, Aekatperone does not reach far into the extracellular end of the pocket to interact with R306 (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: During MD simulations of Aekatperone in its SUR1 binding pocket, Aekatperone remained within the pocket throughout the 500 ns simulation time in all five runs (a total of 2.5 μs) but exhibited some flexibility.
source: During MD simulations of Aekatperone in its SUR1 binding pocket, Aekatperone remained within the pocket throughout the 500 ns simulation time in all five runs (a total of 2.5 μs) but exhibited some flexibility.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the MD simulation results.

claim: The imidazole ring of Aekatperone (group e) displays considerable conformational freedom during MD simulations.
source: The positions of the centers of mass for each part, shown in corresponding colors in Figure 6A, indicate that while the positional distributions of most groups are relatively localized, group e, which corresponds to the imidazole ring, displays considerable conformational freedom.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Y377A, R1246A, and R1300A mutations all significantly decreased the dose-dependent inhibitory effects of Aekatperone.
source: Consistent with our structural model, Y377A, R1246A, and R1300A all significantly decreased the dose-dependent inhibitory effects of Aekatperone (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Rb+ efflux assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The Y377A and R1300A mutations are detrimental to the ability of Aekatperone to inhibit the channel even at the highest concentration of Aekatperone (50 μM) tested.
